records.title: The Pied Piper of Hamelin (Der Rattenfänger von Hameln)
records.summary: In the year 1284, the Lower Saxon town of Hamelin on the Weser River was infested by a catastrophic plague of rats. A mysterious stranger clad in multicolored (pied) clothing offered to rid the town of all vermin for a negotiated sum. Drawing a silver pipe from his coat, his enchanting piping lured every rat into the Weser River, where they drowned. When the greedy town council reneged on payment, the piper returned on Saint John and Paul's Day (June 26), playing a soft, hypnotic melody. One hundred and thirty children followed him out of town toward the Koppen mountain, where the rock opened and swallowed them forever, leaving only two children behind—one lame and one mute—to tell the terrifying tale.
records.historical_period: High Medieval Era (June 26, 1284 town chronicle record, compiled by Brothers Grimm KHM 245)
records.region_or_community: Hamelin, Lower Saxony, Weser River Valley

records.title: The Lorelei of the Rhine Rock
records.summary: Perched atop a towering, narrow slate rock cliff rising 132 meters above the treacherous rapids of the Middle Rhine River near Sankt Goarshausen, the Lorelei (Loreley) is an enchanting water nymph with cascading golden hair. Comb in hand, she sings intoxicatingly beautiful melodies at twilight. Bewitched by her celestial singing, Rhine barge boatmen and sailors gaze upward at her golden beauty rather than watching the treacherous reefs below, crashing their vessels against the jagged submerged rocks and drowning in the swirling whirlpools of the Rhine Gorge.
alternate_names: The Rhine Siren of Sankt Goarshausen
records.historical_period: German Romantic Era (Clemens Brentano 1801, immortalized 1824 by Heinrich Heine)

records.title: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (Schneewittchen)
records.summary: Recorded by the Brothers Grimm as KHM 53, a beautiful princess with skin as white as snow, lips as red as blood, and hair as black as ebony incurs the murderous vanity of her wicked stepmother. When the Queen's magical talking mirror declares Snow White fairer than she, the Queen orders a huntsman to kill her in the wild forest and bring back her lungs and liver. Sparing her life, the huntsman lets her flee into the seven mountains, where she finds refuge in the cottage of seven industrious mining dwarfs. Disguised as an old peddler woman, the Queen poisons her with a poisoned comb, suffocating bodice, and a red poisoned apple, placing Snow White in a glass coffin until a prince's servants dislodge the apple piece.
records.historical_period: 18th–19th Century German Oral Tradition (published 1812 by Brothers Grimm KHM 53)
records.region_or_community: Hesse and Spessart forest regions, Central Germany

records.title: Hansel and Gretel and the Gingerbread Witch
records.summary: During a devastating famine, a poor woodcutter's callous second wife persuades him to abandon his children, Hansel and Gretel, deep in the dark forest. While Hansel's white pebble trail leads them home on the first attempt, birds consume his breadcrumb trail on the second. Lost in the woods, they are drawn to a magical cottage constructed of gingerbread cakes, sugar windows, and marzipan. Welcomed inside by an elderly woman, she reveals herself as a cannibalistic forest witch who cages Hansel to fatten him and forces Gretel into servitude. When the witch prepares her brick oven to bake them, clever Gretel feigns ignorance of how to test the heat, tricking the witch into leaning forward and shoving her into the blazing oven.
alternate_names: The Gingerbread House in the Woods
records.historical_period: 18th–19th Century Folk Tradition (published 1812 Brothers Grimm KHM 15)

records.title: Rumpelstiltskin (Rumpelstilzchen)
records.summary: A boastful, foolish miller lies to the King that his beautiful daughter can spin straw into pure gold. Locked inside a tower room full of straw under threat of execution, a diminutive imp appears, offering to spin the straw for her necklace, and on the second night for her ring. On the third night, having nothing left to trade, she promises her firstborn child. Married to the King, a royal infant is born a year later. When the imp arrives to claim the child, he relents on one condition: if she can discover his name within three days, she may keep her baby. On the third night, a royal messenger discovers the imp dancing around a campfire in the woods chanting: 'Today I bake, tomorrow brew, the next I'll bring the Queen's child too, for little does anybody wot that Rumpelstiltskin is my name!'
alternate_names: The Little Imp of the Spinning Wheel
records.historical_period: Renaissance to 19th Century German Oral Lore (published 1812 Grimm KHM 55)

records.title: The Town Musicians of Bremen (Die Bremer Stadtmusikanten)
records.summary: Discarded and facing slaughter due to old age by their ungrateful owners, four domestic animals—a donkey, a hound, a cat, and a rooster—decide to journey together to the free Hanseatic city of Bremen to become town musicians. Lost in the woods as night falls, the animals spot a light in a cozy cottage, discovering a gang of robbers feasting at a loaded table. Stacking themselves one upon the other—the dog on the donkey's back, the cat on the dog, and the rooster on the cat's head—they burst through the glass window braying, barking, mewing, and crowing simultaneously. Terrified by the monstrous silhouette, the robbers flee into the forest, leaving the four companion animals to live together in comfort and fellowship.
records.historical_period: 19th Century Northern German Folk Tradition (published 1819 Grimm KHM 27)
records.region_or_community: Free Hanseatic City of Bremen and Lower Saxony

records.title: The Wild Hunt of Wotan (Die Wilde Jagd)
records.summary: Deeply rooted in ancient Germanic paganism and surviving into modern German peasant folklore, Die Wilde Jagd (The Wild Hunt) is a terrifying phantom procession led by the Norse-Germanic god Wotan (Odin), Frau Holle, or the cursed huntsman Hackelberg. Sweeping through the nocturnal skies during the Twelve Holy Nights of Christmas (Rauhnächte) and Midwinter storms, the ghostly host consists of phantom black hounds with glowing eyes, skeletal huntsmen, and screaming Valkyrie spirits. Countryfolk warned that travelers caught on lonely forest roads must fling themselves facedown on the earth and remain motionless, lest they be swept up by the spectral vortex and compelled to ride with the dead for eternity.
records.historical_period: Ancient Germanic Paganism to Living Alpine/Bavarian Folk Tradition
records.region_or_community: Black Forest, Harz Mountains, and Bavarian Alps

records.title: The Legend of Doctor Faustus and Mephistopheles
records.summary: Based loosely on the historical renaissance astrologer and alchemist Johann Georg Faust (c. 1480–1540), Faustus is a brilliant scholar in Wittenberg who exhausts all human knowledge of philosophy, medicine, law, and theology. Yearning for boundless worldly power, forbidden magical knowledge, and physical pleasures, Faustus summons the demon Mephistopheles in a dark forest crossroad. Signing a pact with a drop of his own blood, Faustus exchanges his eternal soul for twenty-four years of absolute demonic service. Touring the courts of Europe, conjuring Helen of Troy, and mastering sorcery, Faustus's contract reaches its terrifying deadline in an inn in Staufen im Breisgau, where demons tear his body apart at midnight.
records.historical_period: Renaissance Era (1587 Frankfurt Faustbuch, immortalized by J. W. von Goethe 1808)
records.region_or_community: Wittenberg, Saxony-Anhalt and Staufen im Breisgau, Baden-Württemberg

records.title: The Water Nixie of the Black Forest (Nix und Nixe)
records.summary: Dwelling in the dark, cold glacial tarns, mountain rivers, and cascading millponds of the Black Forest (Schwarzwald), Nix and Nixe are shapeshifting Germanic water spirits. Male nixes manifest as old bearded men with green teeth or handsome youths recognized by wet hemlines on their coats, while female nixes appear as delicate river maidens with webbed fingers who attend village dances in elegant gowns. In Black Forest folklore, the Nix is a master of the golden harp whose seductive aquatic melodies entrance humans to step into deep water. Villagers respected strict taboos: throwing bread and pins into millponds before swimming, and leaving the water before dusk when the Nix claims his annual tribute.
records.historical_period: Traditional Germanic Folklore (Grimm Deutsche Sagen No. 62)
records.region_or_community: Schwarzwald (Black Forest) and Upper Rhine, Baden-Württemberg
community_attributions: Black Forest millers and timber floaters

records.title: The Kobold of the Harz Mountains (Hüttengeist)
records.summary: A fixture of medieval German folklore, the Kobold exists in two traditions: the domestic house spirit (Heinzelmännchen) who cleans hearths and feeds horses in exchange for a bowl of sweet milk porridge, and the mining subterranean sprite (Bergkobold or Hüttengeist) who haunts the deep silver and copper shafts of the Harz Mountains. Miners in Rammelsberg and Goslar reported hearing the unseen creature tapping against rock faces with a miniature pickaxe. While friendly to respectful miners by knocking to warn of imminent tunnel cave-ins, the creature was notoriously vengeful toward foul-mouthed miners, extinguishing oil lanterns and siphoning valuable silver ore into worthless, toxic cobalt-arsenic rock (from which the chemical element cobalt takes its name).
records.historical_period: Medieval Mining Boom (c. 12th–16th Century Harz silver mines)
records.region_or_community: Harz Mountain mining district, Lower Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt
